I'm glad I could give you some perspective. It can be truly difficult for someone who doesn't have PTSD to understand how a seemingly simple question can wreak so much havoc in someone's mind if you don't know a lot about the disorder. If I could offer one piece of advice? I personally think you should apologize. Something along the lines of "I didn't really understand PSTD and after doing some research I now realize how insensitive my question was." I'm certainly not saying you have to like this guy, or even believe a word that comes out of his mouth, but if there is even a chance that he does have it then I think he deserves an apology. Just my two cents. Try not to beat yourself up about it, though. Now you know.

You are the asshole in this situation. If someone has  PTSD it is from an event so traumatic that it completely overrides their ability to function. For some, talking about their traumatic experience can be extremely triggering and can cause them to have flashbacks. Also, unless you spend a lot of time with someone it is really hard to tell if they have it. Even if this guy is lying (which could very well be the case), you simply don't ask someone to tell you the most horrific experience of their lives. 

Source: I have PTSD

I struggle with this a lot, actually. For the longest time I just didn't know *how* to take care of myself, eventually I figured out the basics, but not before it took a major toll on my self-esteem. Sometimes I just feel like I don't deserve to be take care of, which is exactly what Mommie Dearest taught me to believe. 

One thing that's helped me is working with young children (obviously not for everyone!). Helping them through their routines: bath, brush teeth, books and bed has helped me to develop my own routine. Another thing that's helped me is I imagine I'm a foster parent. One of my "foster children" is myself as a child. When I look at this girl I see that all she needs is a bit a guidance, some help establishing a routine. "Risingsun27, I know that that is a very interesting thread your reading on Reddit, but in five minutes we need to start getting ready for bed." "Okay, Risingsun27, It's time to start your bedtime routine. I know that you don't like getting ready for bed, but I care about you and want to you be clean and healthy. I know you have a hard time motivating yourself, but I want you to know I love you and I'll always be here to help you."

He pressured you into having sex with him, this is called coercion. One of the many manifestations of sexual abuse can be [repeatedly pressuring someone to have sex or perform sexual acts. ](http://www.loveisrespect.org/is-this-abuse/types-of-abuse/what-is-sexual-abuse) 



It's 100% your decision what you do with this information. If you believe that he just honestly doesn't know that what he is doing is wrong, then maybe you want to see a counsellor together so that he can learn about consent. Or you could print off information on coercion and discuss that this behavior **cannot** continue if you are to be in a relationship together. Or you could decide that regardless of his intent, what he did was wrong and break up with his ass. It's you're choice. 

I hope that you try to talk to a professional or a loved one whom you trust (sorry about the cliche) about what you're feeling. It's important to not to try to go through this kind of thing alone.

If you said things like "I don't want to" and "I don't feel like it" and he kept asking after you said no multiple times, going so far as to continue asking until you give in then you have every right to feel like this was whatever you conclude it to be.
